body:
For infant sleep, the basic setup is a firm, flat mattress with a fitted sheet and an otherwise bare crib. No loose blankets, pillows, bumpers, stuffed animals, sleep positioners, or added padding.

The harder part is knowing whether the setup you have actually meets that standard.

Before your baby's first night in the crib, check four things:

  • Is the mattress firm and flat?
  • Does it fit securely inside the crib?
  • Does the fitted sheet stay smooth and tight?
  • Is the mattress height appropriate for your baby's current mobility?

Here is how to check each one.

1. Press the mattress before you use it

"Firm" can be vague, so use your hands.

Press down on several areas of the mattress. It should feel supportive rather than plush or sink-in soft. The surface should remain flat instead of creating a deep depression.

Then look across the mattress from the side.

You should not see:

  • sagging
  • dips
  • folded or raised corners
  • extra padding
  • mattress toppers
  • blankets placed underneath or on top to make it softer

Adult mattresses are often designed to contour around the body. That softness is not what you are looking for in an infant sleep surface.

The crib mattress should be firm and flat on its own. You should not have to add anything to make it feel more comfortable.

2. Check the mattress inside the actual crib

Do not rely only on the words "crib mattress" on the packaging.

Once the mattress is installed, check all four edges. It should sit securely inside the crib rather than looking undersized, shifting around easily, or leaving obvious gaps around the sides.

Try moving it gently with your hands. The mattress should feel like it belongs in the frame, not like something that has been made to fit.

This check is especially useful if the crib and mattress were purchased separately.

If the fit looks loose or improvised, stop and confirm that the mattress dimensions are appropriate for your specific crib before using it for sleep.

3. Check the fitted sheet after it is on

A fitted sheet has a simple job: cover the mattress securely without creating loose fabric on the sleep surface.

After putting it on, run your hand across the mattress.

The sheet should:

  • lie smooth
  • stay attached at the corners
  • fit the mattress's size and depth
  • remain snug when you gently pull on it

If fabric is bunching, corners keep coming loose, or you have to force the sheet onto the mattress, check the sizing.

There is no need to add another layer over or underneath it. For infant sleep, the mattress and fitted sheet are the sleep surface.

4. Look inside the crib and remove the extras

Once the mattress and sheet are set up, look at what else is inside the crib.

For infant sleep, remove:

  • pillows
  • loose blankets
  • quilts and comforters
  • crib bumpers
  • stuffed animals
  • sleep positioners
  • decorative cushions
  • added mattress padding

This can make a styled nursery look surprisingly empty.

That is okay.

Put the personality around the crib instead of inside the sleep space. Rugs, curtains, wall art, paint, lighting, and furniture can make the room feel warm without adding objects where your baby sleeps.

The crib itself does not need decoration during sleep.

When should you lower the crib mattress?

Do not rely only on your baby's age.

Watch what your baby can do.

The highest mattress position is generally useful during the earliest stage, when your baby is less mobile and easier access makes placing them in the crib more convenient.

As your baby becomes stronger and more mobile, the mattress needs to move down according to your crib manufacturer's instructions.

Pay attention when your baby begins showing new abilities such as:

  • rolling
  • pushing up strongly
  • sitting with support
  • reaching higher
  • becoming noticeably more active in the crib

The useful rule is to reassess before a new ability creates a problem, rather than waiting until afterward.

Each time your baby's mobility changes, check the mattress height again.

When should you move from a bassinet to a crib?

There is no single age that applies to every bassinet.

Instead, check your bassinet's manufacturer instructions for its:

  • weight limit
  • size or growth limits
  • rolling restrictions
  • pushing-up restrictions
  • other developmental cutoffs

If your baby reaches one of those limits, it is time to stop using that bassinet even if they still sleep comfortably in it.

It is also worth reviewing the limits as soon as your baby starts becoming more mobile. Rolling attempts, pushing up, and increased movement can arrive quickly.

You do not have to wait until the bassinet feels obviously too small before preparing the crib.

Can a newborn sleep in a crib?

Yes. A crib can be used from the newborn stage when it is an approved sleep space and is set up with a firm, flat mattress, a fitted sheet, and no loose items inside.

Some families use a bassinet first because it takes up less space or makes overnight care more convenient.

A bassinet is not a required stage before a crib.

If the crib works better for your room and routine, it can be your baby's sleep space from the beginning.

Moving to a crib does not have to end room-sharing

A crib transition and a bedroom transition are separate decisions.

If your baby has outgrown the bassinet but you still want to room-share, the crib can go in your bedroom if you have enough space to use it safely.

Before moving it in, measure more than the footprint of the crib.

Make sure you still have enough room to:

  • get in and out of bed
  • walk around the crib
  • reach your baby comfortably
  • handle nighttime feeds
  • move through the room without squeezing past furniture

A crib that technically fits may still be awkward if it blocks the way you actually use the room at night.

What if the room is cold?

Do not solve a cold room by adding a loose blanket to the crib.

Keep the sleep space bare and focus instead on how your baby is dressed for the room.

That lets you address temperature without adding loose bedding to the mattress.

Do you need a mattress topper?

No.

The crib mattress should provide the appropriate sleep surface on its own. Adding a topper, folded blanket, cushion, or other padding makes the surface softer rather than improving the setup.

If the mattress seems uncomfortable because it feels much firmer than your own bed, remember that infant mattresses are not supposed to feel like adult mattresses.

Firmness is intentional.

A 60-second crib check before bedtime

You do not need to rethink the entire nursery every night.

Use this quick check whenever you set up a new crib, change bedding, lower the mattress, or notice a new developmental milestone:

  1. Look inside. Remove everything except the mattress and fitted sheet.
  2. Press the mattress. Confirm that it feels firm and lies flat.
  3. Check the edges. Make sure the mattress sits securely without obvious gaps or shifting.
  4. Run your hand over the sheet. It should be smooth and snug.
  5. Check the mattress height. Ask whether your baby's newest movements mean it needs to be lowered.
  6. Review the bassinet if you still use one. Check whether growth, rolling, pushing up, or manufacturer limits mean it is time to switch.

That is the crib setup worth getting right.

You do not need to make the sleep space softer, fuller, or more decorated. You need a mattress that is firm and flat, a sheet that fits properly, a crib that is set up for your baby's current stage, and nothing unnecessary inside it.
